summary:
Kieran Klaassen, working alone at Every, is rebuilding Cora, an agent-native email client that runs on desktop, phone, CLI, and inside tools like Codex. His two-year trajectory shifted the dominant bottleneck from bad code (fixed with agents, skills, and review) to weak plans, then to deciding what to build (fixed by dogfooding), and finally to repetition, which he solved by extracting taste into a persistent memory system. That memory system is the seed of compound engineering: a brainstorm-plan-work-review-polish-compound loop he calls the "human-AI sandwich," with the human's brain on at the start to frame the problem and at the end to apply taste, while the middle runs autonomously, often overnight in parallel.

His hard rule is a 50/50 time split, half building the feature, half teaching the system what went wrong. He argues this is token-efficient because stored solution documents eliminate future correction passes and web-research detours. He demonstrates the Compound Engineering / Compound Product plugin: CE IDEATE turns a messy backlog into argued, OKR-scored ideas; CE DOC REVIEW asks sharp, deliberately few questions whose answers are then compounded so they are never asked again; CE BRAINSTORM is a "brain on" command that pulls compound knowledge and persona differences; and /LFG is the autonomous loop that plans, reviews, tests, opens a PR, runs before/after screenshots, and dogfoods for hours.

Klaassen emphasizes that polish is not QA but raising the bar, and that when an LFG run returns work that "just works," the polish pass is where taste gets exercised and extracted. He closes by urging builders to extract every repeated lesson, document the thinking rather than only the code, run postmortems on agent decisions, and invert the standard success bar: each shipped feature should make the next one easier to build, not harder, because judgment is the fixed bottleneck while implementation keeps getting cheaper.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Shipping without writing or reading the code
sections.summary: Klaassen introduces himself at Every and states the central claim: he has not written a line of code this year and barely reads what is produced, yet he ships and is proud of both the code and the product (Cora). He previews a talk with two halves — the trajectory that got him here, and day-to-day practices — and explicitly rejects hype framing in favor of workflow that survives newer and bigger models.

sections.title: Building an email client alone, on purpose
sections.summary: Introduces Every as a future-of-work lab and Cora as a one-engineer agent-native email inbox rebuilt from January, running on Rails/React across desktop, phone, CLI, and Codex/MCPs. He frames the solo setup as deliberate: a former YC engineer and founder deliberately inverting the hiring playbook to see how far AI can go before a team is needed.

sections.title: The bottleneck moved from code to plans to judgment
sections.summary: Walks through the two-year ladder of bottlenecks. Bad code and hallucinations were fixed with agents, skills, and review. Then weak plans became the limit; good plans unlocked larger work. Then deciding what to build dominated and was improved by dogfooding. Finally repetition was the remaining pain, which is what forced a memory system.

sections.title: Where compound engineering came from
sections.summary: Pitches compound engineering as the system that emerged from solving repetition. Implementation is 'mostly solved,' but judgments and taste are not. The goal is to keep extracting taste into the system until the next brainstorm already contains prior thinking, enabling a single engineer with a compounding system to beat full AI-using teams.

sections.title: The loop, and the human at both ends
sections.summary: Defines the core loop — brainstorm, plan, work, review, polish, compound, repeat — and calls it the 'human-AI sandwich': brain on at the start (decide the problem) and at the end (apply taste / raise the bar), with hours of autonomous middle. Stresses that letting go overnight in parallel requires the system to be set up correctly.

sections.title: Half your time teaching the system what it got wrong
sections.summary: States the 50/50 rule: half the time on whether the feature was delivered, half on teaching the system anything it got wrong. He argues storing knowledge as solution documents in the repo is actually more token-efficient because the next run avoids review, correction, and web research.

sections.title: Why stored solutions are cheaper in tokens
sections.summary: Pushes back on the 'but tokens' objection with research showing right answers already in-context cut out review, correction, and deep-research detours. Frames the deeper reason: human brain capacity is fixed, models keep improving, so keep extracting until the whole middle runs itself and surprises you.

sections.title: The plugin, and building it while building the product
sections.summary: Introduces the Compound Engineering plugin (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, +10) and Compound Product with co-contributor Trevin Chow. Notes that hundreds of thousands use it daily, that he never marketed it, and that the universal compounding concept extends beyond engineering to PMs, designers, and knowledge workers.

sections.title: Turning a backlog into an argued set of ideas
sections.summary: Live-walks CE IDEATE: hands it Cora v1→v2 plus the messy open-ticket backlog across GitHub, Linear, Slack, Intercom. It outputs a clean argued HTML page, can be pointed at OKRs and past learnings, and the doc can be dropped into a design tool for a PowerPoint with an XY matrix of what to work on next.

sections.title: Sharp questions on a document, and only enough of them
sections.summary: Shows CE DOC REVIEW on a PRD, emphasizing sharp questions deliberately few in number. Answers are then compounded so the same question never appears again. Argues against 30-question overloads: the goal is the best work, not the most answers, and the doc itself compounds.

sections.title: The overnight loop, and polish as raising the bar
sections.summary: Demonstrates CE BRAINSTORM as a 'brain on' command for problems too big to describe: it pulls compound knowledge, persona differences, and asks only the questions needed to do the work. Then introduces /LFG, the full autonomous loop that plans, reviews, tests, opens a PR, and dogfoods for hours.

sections.title: Doing this without the plugin; the next feature should be easier than this one
sections.summary: Notes you don't need the plugin — you can store learnings in files. The through-line: extraction compounds until the next feature is easier to build because the last one shipped, inverting how complexity normally accumulates.

sections.title: Polish on the LFG PR, documenting reasoning, and the inverted success bar
sections.summary: Closes the loop by showing what polish actually does: run /LFG's PR side-by-side with the product in Cursor, raise the bar (e.g. flag a duplicate logo mark), then run CE Compound so the rule is stored for next time. Argues polish is not QA but taste at the finish. Leaves the audience with three takeaways: extract every repetition, document the reasoning (not just the code) and write postmortems on agent decisions so behavior changes next time, and reapply the 50/50 rule at every interaction. Closes with the inverted success bar — the next feature should be easier because this one shipped — and the bet that implementation keeps getting cheaper while judgment stays fixed.

demonstrations: CE IDEATE: dumps open GitHub/Linear/Slack/Intercom tickets and outputs an argued HTML page of ideas scored against OKRs and prior learnings
CE DOC REVIEW: runs on a PRD and returns a small set of sharp questions; answers are then compounded so the same question is not asked twice
CE BRAINSTORM ("brain on"): blocks off focus time, pulls compound knowledge plus persona differences, and produces a brainstorm document
/LFG: the autonomous execution loop that plans, reviews, tests, opens a PR with before/after screenshots, and dogfoods for hours
Polish pass on an /LFG PR: human runs it in Cursor side-by-side with the product, raises the bar (e.g. flags a duplicate logo mark), then runs CE Compound so the rule is stored for future design work

organization.name: Every
organization.summary: Every is an independent media and software company founded in 2020 by CEO Dan Shipper. The official about page says it publishes a daily newsletter on what comes next in technology and also builds software products, courses, and AI consulting. First-party guides state Every runs five products—including Cora—with primarily single-person engineering teams. Kieran Klaassen is GM of Cora and an entrepreneur in residence; compound engineering is the methodology he invented while building Cora, published as an Every guide and the EveryInc GitHub plugin. Compound Engineering is a method, not a company.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. every.to, the about page, Cora, and the EveryInc plugin repo are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
